newsitem.title: USA: Latin American woes won't derail reform process.
newsitem.headline: Latin American woes won't derail reform process.

text.p: Growing labor unrest and a backlash against fiscal austerity measures in Latin America may slow the pace of economic reforms in the region but it won't derail the process, emerging market experts said.

"You may see some backsliding or slowing down of the reform process but if you look at the whole thing in context, no one is really going way back," said Susan Kaufman Purcell, vice president at the Society of the Americas.
Certainly, populist sounding rhetoric has begun to take hold in countries throughout the region.

In Colombia, a massive nationwide strike protesting wage increases of 13.5 percent proposed by the government instead of the 21.5 percent wage increase requested by labor unions continued as talks with government ministers broke down.

And in Ecuador, a nationwide strike against increases in public sector tariffs and subsidy cuts, along with alleged government corruption, resulted in the removal last week of the country's president, Abdala Bucaram, on the grounds of mental incompetence.

"What the real problem is is that people in society feel that others are benefitting from reforms but they're not, and so at some point, depending on how much they are pressed, they will take to the streets," said Purcell.
Despite the recent backlash against tough government austerity measures and smaller-than-expected spending increases, emerging market experts believe market reforms will continue, albeit slowly.

"The alternative to tough economic reforms is populism, and that is a bankrupt idea in Latin America," said Thomas Trebat, managing director for emerging market research at Citicorp Securities in New York.
In the case of Ecuador, he explained that Bucaram was trying to do too much too fast.

"There can be bumps in the road; there can be setbacks, and there can be revisions, but policy reforms in Latin America will continue wherever there is a strong social consensus behind them, and that consensus exists in Ecuador to move slowly and to move gradually," Trebat said.
Sources said that even the populist agenda of Venezuelan President Rafael Caldera fell by the wayside after he tried to buck the tide by implementing foreign exchange controls and price controls.
Indeed, investors started to move capital back into Venezuela after Caldera reversed his stance.
Still, some experts warned that the next wave of reform in Latin America would be far more difficult.

"There has been a tremendous return to capital over the last six years throughout the globe and now it looks like labor wants its share of that chunk," said Gary Evans, senior emerging market debt strategist at Lehman Brothers.

Though the initial phase of reforms in countries such as Argentina and Brazil was extremely popular because it reduced hyperinflation and thus increased individual purchasing power, experts said the next stage would be more difficult because it will entail public sector layoffs and loss of benefits.
For example, they said labor reform in Argentina is likely to continue to meet widespread opposition given the country's nearly 18 percent unemployment rate.

"In the case of (Argentine President Carlos) Menem, he has little real room because of the 18 percent unemployment. The real issue is that it is going to be very hard to convince labor unions with 18 percent unemployment to give up any benefits," said Riordan Roett, head of the Latin American Studies Program at Johns Hopkins University in Maryland.
Venezuela is another country where the the reform process may slow if lower-than-expected public sector wage increases result in labor strife.
At the same time, experts cautioned that Venezuela needs to be careful not to use windfall oil profits to pay for those public sector wage increases.

"Venezuela has to be diligent in not living it up with the huge windfalls of oil. The problem there is they have to walk a fine line of improving the living standard of Venezuelans, and at the same time maintain the direction of market reform," said Evans of Lehman.

While some benefitted tremendously from the drop in inflation rates as they saw their purchasing power increase, experts said low rates of economic growth have not been enough to increase the income per capita in much of Latin America.

"Real wages have to grow in these countries," said Evans, pointing out that countries are recognizing that they need to invest more in the social infrastructure, and that the World Bank and international financial institutions need to take the lead in financing things such as health and education.

"On average, all these economies look better, but the real gains have been accruing to a fairly limited sector of the population and everybody else feels worse off," said one emerging market fund manager at a major U.S. bank, who did not want to be identified.

As for a solution, experts stressed that economies need to grow and the ever-pervasive inequality in income distribution in Latin America needs to narrow for societies to become more amenable to furthering economic reforms.

"The income distribution is still unfavorable. Therefore what is necessary in the second phase is rapid growth in order to increase savings," said Albert Fishlow, senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.

Evans added: "How the growth comes is a different story. Is it going to come through the export sector and investment? Or is it going to come through consumption? That is very key in terms of long-term sustainability."
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1946 ))
